items.prompt: Which stage answers 'does this compile or package correctly?'
choices: Build
Test
Production deploy
items.explanation: The build stage turns source into a package, so a compile failure stops there.

items.prompt: Which stage checks that the change behaves correctly?
choices: Build
Production deploy
Test
items.explanation: The test stage runs the code to see what it does.

items.prompt: What does deploying to staging check?
choices: That the commit message is well written
That it works outside a developer's machine
That the database has enough free disk space
items.explanation: Staging is a rehearsal outside any laptop, so environment-specific bugs show up there.

items.prompt: What is staging?
choices: The live app that real users touch
A backup copy of all the stored source code
A rehearsal copy used before production
items.explanation: Staging is the practice copy placed before the real thing.

items.prompt: What is production?
choices: The real app that users touch
A rehearsal copy used for tests
A saved snapshot of a change
items.explanation: Production is the live environment that real users use.

items.prompt: What is an artifact?
choices: A bug that the test stage found in the build
The built package that moves between places
A rule that halts the pipeline when tests fail
items.explanation: An artifact is the already-built package that travels through staging and production.

items.prompt: In the toy factory, which station is the test stage?
choices: The truck that ships finished toys
The worker who assembles the toy
The inspector who checks each toy
items.explanation: The inspector is the picture for tests: each toy is checked before moving on.

items.prompt: A stage is only useful if its failures do what?
choices: Get logged and forgotten
Actually stop the pipeline
Retry forever without limit
items.explanation: A check that cannot stop anything protects nothing.

items.prompt: A bug appears only when the app runs against realistic data on a shared server, never on a laptop. Which stage is built to catch it first?
choices: Build, which packages the code for later stages
Deploy to staging, which runs off a laptop
Test, which checks behaviour on small fixture data
Production, which has the most realistic data
items.explanation: Staging exists for exactly this class: bugs that need a real environment. Tests on small fixtures and builds on a laptop cannot see it.
items.reference:
One stage, one question
🔨 build: does it compile and package?
🔍 test: does it behave correctly?
🏪 staging: does it work off a laptop?
🚚 production: the live app users touch
Why: each stage catches one class of problem, and only works if its failure stops the line.
items.learnMore:
Each stage catches one thing

A build failure tells you nothing about behaviour, and a passing test says nothing about the real environment. Skipping a stage does not save time, it removes the only catcher for that class of bug.

Common mistake

Thinking a later stage will catch what an earlier one was skipped for.
items.reflection: Think of any process with checkpoints (airport security, a kitchen pass, a proofreader). What does each checkpoint catch that the one before it cannot?

items.prompt: A missing bracket stops the app from compiling. Which stage should halt the line, and why is that cheapest?
choices: Test, because only tests ever read the source code
Staging, because only it runs outside of a laptop
Production, because users report errors the fastest
Build, since later stages need a working package
items.explanation: A build failure means there is no artifact to test or deploy, so stopping at the first stage wastes nothing and ships nothing.

choices: Bugs that appear only off a developer's laptop
Bugs that prevent the whole app from compiling
Bugs in the logic of one small helper function
Bugs in the wording of a commit message line
items.explanation: Compile errors are caught by build and function logic by tests. Only staging exercises a real environment.

items.prompt: Which pairing of stage and silent-bypass cost matches the unit's table?
choices: Build bypassed: environment-specific bugs reach production
Staging bypassed: broken artifacts reach later stages
Test bypassed: bugs reach production undetected
Test bypassed: environment-specific bugs reach production
items.explanation: The table ties each stage to its own cost. Bypassing tests lets behaviour bugs through, while environment bugs belong to staging.

items.prompt: CI answers which question?
choices: Where do we deploy it?
Is this change good?
Who approves the release?
items.explanation: CI judges the change: does it build, and does it behave?

items.prompt: CD answers which question?
choices: How does a good change reach production?
Is this change good enough to be merged?
Who wrote this commit and when?
items.explanation: CD is about delivery of a change that CI already judged good.

items.prompt: What does CI stand for?
choices: Constant inspection of builds
Central installation server
Continuous integration
items.explanation: CI is continuous integration.

items.prompt: Which of these is a CI stage?
choices: Test
Production deploy
Rollback
items.explanation: Tests judge the change, which is CI's job.

items.prompt: Which of these is a CD concern?
choices: Judging whether the new code compiles
Moving an approved build to production
Reviewing the code style rules for a file
items.explanation: Delivery of a judged-good change is CD.

items.prompt: Can CI and CD be separate concerns inside one pipeline?
choices: No, they are one single step
Only when staging is absent
Yes, chained but distinct
items.explanation: A pipeline chains the judging part and the delivering part, and they stay different questions.

items.prompt: What connects CI's verdict to CD's delivery?
choices: The gate between them
The commit message text
The staging database
items.explanation: The gate is the rule that only judged-good changes move on.

items.prompt: A pipeline has great CI but no enforced gate. What happens?
choices: It never ships anything at all
It fixes the bugs by itself
It can still ship broken code
items.explanation: A verdict that nothing obeys protects no one.

items.prompt: A team's CI is thorough, but the deploy job starts on every push regardless of CI's result. What is missing?
choices: An enforced gate linking CI's verdict to CD
More tests inside the existing CI stage
A faster production deploy job overall
A second staging environment for rehearsals
items.explanation: The verdict exists but nothing obeys it. More tests or more environments do not change that.
items.reference:
Judge, then deliver
⚖️ CI: is this change good?
🚚 CD: how does a good change reach users?
🚪 the gate links the two
🔕 an ignored verdict makes CI decoration
Why: CI only protects users if CD obeys its verdict.
items.learnMore:
Two chained concerns

Thorough tests are worth nothing if the deploy job starts anyway. The link between the verdict and the delivery is the gate, and it needs enforcing as much as the tests need writing.

Common mistake

Investing in more tests while the gate that obeys them stays optional.
items.reflection: Think of a restaurant where one person tastes the dish and another carries it out. What breaks if the carrier never asks whether the taster approved?

items.prompt: Which statement correctly splits a pipeline's work between CI and CD?
choices: CI moves the change to users; CD judges the change
CI builds the app; CD writes the tests for it
CI judges the change; CD ships a judged-good one
CI and CD both judge, differing only in speed
items.explanation: Judging versus delivering is the split. Reversing it, or calling both judges, loses the point of the gate.

items.prompt: A team adds 500 more tests but leaves the test step bypassable. Does the production deploy get safer?
choices: Yes, since every added test blocks the deploy by itself
Yes, because CD re-runs every test at production
No, because unit tests only ever run in staging
No, a bypassed verdict is ignored however thorough
items.explanation: CI quality only counts when the gate honours it. A bypass makes extra tests decoration.

items.prompt: Every test passed, but the production deploy died halfway on a network error. Which concern failed?
choices: CI, because the tests passed too early
CD, because the good change never arrived
CI, because the build must be repeated
Neither, because failures only belong to staging
items.explanation: The change was judged good, so CI did its job. Getting it to users is CD.

items.prompt: What does continue-on-error do?
choices: Retries the failed step again and again until it passes
Hides the step's logs from the dashboard view
Lets the pipeline go on after a step fails
items.explanation: The flag tells the pipeline to carry on past a failed step.

items.prompt: continue-on-error is meant to be what?
choices: A permanent default setting
A temporary escape hatch
A speed optimization
items.explanation: It is for a specific, short-lived situation.

items.prompt: What can a bypass silently turn a safety gate into?
choices: A step that always reports success
A step that runs twice on every commit
A step that runs faster than it did
items.explanation: With the flag set, the step can fail and the pipeline still shows it as passed.

items.prompt: What should come with a temporary override?
choices: A louder colour on the dashboard
A ticket and a removal plan
A longer test timeout
items.explanation: Without a plan to remove it, a temporary fix becomes permanent.

items.prompt: Which check is a reasonable place for a temporary bypass?
choices: The main test suite itself
The production deploy step itself
A known-flaky, low-stakes check
items.explanation: The bypass belongs where failure does not mean broken code.

items.prompt: In the toy factory, the bypass is like what?
choices: A note telling the inspector to pass every toy
A second inspector joining the line to help out
A faster conveyor belt for the toys
items.explanation: The note makes the inspector's stamp meaningless.

items.prompt: Why did the note stay on the desk?
choices: The factory deletes notes weekly
Nobody tracked its removal
The machines required it to run
items.explanation: No owner and no date means no one takes it down.

items.prompt: What is the practical skill this unit builds?
choices: Giving every temporary override an expiration plan
Never using any flag anywhere in a pipeline's config
Running the tests only once a week
items.explanation: Overrides are fine when they have a ticket, an owner, and a date.

items.prompt: One team puts continue-on-error on a lint step with a ticket due in two weeks. Another puts it on the test suite with no ticket. Which is the real problem?
choices: The lint step, since any flag on any step is unsafe
Both equally, because tickets never get closed
Neither, since both pipelines still show green
The test suite, a correctness gate without a plan
items.explanation: The gate and the plan matter, not the flag. A style check with a ticket is the legitimate case.
items.reference:
A bypass is a loan
🏷️ allowed: known-flaky, low-stakes checks
🚫 not allowed: the main correctness gate
🎫 needs a ticket and an owner
📅 needs a date it comes out
Why: an override without an expiry plan outlives its reason and becomes a permanent gap.
items.learnMore:
Where the flag belongs

A style check can tolerate failure for a while because a violation does not mean broken code. The test suite cannot, because it is the gate for broken code. What separates them is the gate and the plan, not the flag.

Common mistake

Blaming the flag itself instead of where it sits and whether anyone owns its removal.
items.reflection: Think of a temporary sign you have left up, like a wet paint note or a sticky reminder. What would make sure it actually comes down?

items.prompt: The flaky test behind a bypass was later deleted, but the flag stays on the test step. What state is the pipeline in?
choices: A safe pipeline, since the flaky test is gone
A permanent gap that outlived its reason
A faster pipeline with no change in safety
A pipeline that now blocks on every failure
items.explanation: The reason is gone but the flag is not, so real failures are now ignored too.

choices: A code comment saying to remove it later
A chat message asking someone to remember
A dated ticket with an owner and a review
A line in the next release email
items.explanation: A named owner and a date can be checked. Comments and reminders depend on memory.

items.prompt: Someone proposes banning continue-on-error everywhere. What does the unit recommend instead?
choices: Keep a short, reviewed list of bypassable gates
Accept the ban, since advisory checks do not exist
Allow it everywhere, since reviews slow teams down
Allow it only on the production deploy step
items.explanation: Some checks really are advisory. The skill is being deliberate about which, and visible about why.

items.prompt: What is a gate?
choices: A door with a condition for the next stage
A faster server dedicated to the build stage
A log of past deploys
items.explanation: If the condition fails, the next room does not open.

items.prompt: If a gate's condition fails, what should happen?
choices: The next stage runs anyway
The pipeline restarts from the commit
The next stage does not run
items.explanation: That is the entire purpose of a gate.

items.prompt: What makes a pipeline protective?
choices: The number of stages in total
The gates between stages
The speed of each stage
items.explanation: Stages do the work, but gates decide whether work continues.

items.prompt: If Build fails, what runs next?
choices: The test stage, to see what happens
The production deploy
Nothing, the pipeline halts
items.explanation: A failed build has no artifact for anything later.

items.prompt: Are 'the pipeline finished' and 'every gate passed' the same claim?
choices: No, they are different claims
Yes, they are the identical claim
Only for very fast pipelines
items.explanation: A pipeline can finish after ignoring failures.

items.prompt: A pipeline that always reaches its final stage is what?
choices: The safest possible kind of pipeline design
A list of steps, not a safety mechanism
A requirement for CD
items.explanation: Without halting, results never matter.

items.prompt: Where do failures send the pipeline in the flowchart?
choices: Back to the commit
Forward to staging
To a halt
items.explanation: Each failure arrow ends in a stop.

items.prompt: What belongs between the test and staging stages?
choices: A rebuild
A gate
A rollback
items.explanation: The gate enforces that only passing changes move on.

items.prompt: Build passes, tests fail with continue-on-error on, and staging passes. What happens to the commit?
choices: It halts at the test stage because tests failed
It halts at staging because the tests ran earlier
It reaches production because nothing blocked it
It halts at the build stage because it ran first
items.explanation: The bypass makes the test failure non-blocking, and the other gates pass. This is the incident.
items.reference:
A gate is a door with a condition
🔨 build fails: halt, nothing later runs
🔍 test fails: halt unless bypassed
🏳️ a bypassed step records and continues
🏪 a later blocking gate can still halt
Why: what protects you is the condition between stages, not the stages.
items.learnMore:
Finished is not the same as gated

Reaching the last stage only proves the steps ran in order. The protection comes from each gate refusing to open on a failure, and a bypass changes only the gate it is set on.

Common mistake

Reading a green dashboard as a statement that every check passed.
items.reflection: Think of a door that opens regardless of its lock. What is the lock for, and who would notice it is decorative?

items.prompt: The same bypass is on the tests, tests fail, and now staging also fails. Where does it stop?
choices: At staging, the next gate that still blocks
At the test stage, because tests failed first
At the build stage, because it ran first
It does not stop and reaches production
items.explanation: A bypass affects only the step it is on. Staging has no bypass, so its failure halts the line.

choices: Tests run anyway, since the flag covers all steps
The build gate halts the line before tests run
Tests run first, in parallel with the build
The flag turns the build failure into a pass
items.explanation: The flag lives on one step. Build has no bypass, so nothing after it executes.

items.prompt: Why can a fully green dashboard still hide a failure?
choices: Green only means that the commit was pushed to the repo
Dashboards simply turn green after a short timer runs
Green means the tests were skipped on purpose
A bypassed step reports passed though it failed
items.explanation: The flag changes what the step reports, not what its command did.

items.prompt: How many times should the artifact be built for staging and production?
choices: Twice, once for each
Once
Three times in total
items.explanation: One build, promoted, keeps both environments identical.

items.prompt: What moves through staging and then production?
choices: The same artifact, unchanged
A fresh rebuild for each environment
Only the source code
items.explanation: Promotion means moving the very same package.

items.prompt: What does rebuilding per environment risk?
choices: Faster deploys across the board
Smaller log files
Two subtly different artifacts
items.explanation: Each build can differ from the other.

items.prompt: A matching commit guarantees the same what?
choices: Source
Build output
Runner tool version
items.explanation: Same commit pins the source, not what a build makes of it.

items.prompt: 'Tested in staging' should be a claim about what?
choices: A similar-looking rebuild made much later
The literal thing that reaches production
The developer's laptop
items.explanation: That is what promotion buys you.

items.prompt: What is the everyday picture of promotion?
choices: Pack a brand new fresh box for every room
Throw the box away after staging
Inspect the same sealed box in each room
items.explanation: The sealed box stays the same box.

items.prompt: Which can differ between two builds of one commit?
choices: Dependency versions resolved at build time
The exact commit hash of the source code files
The branch name in Git
items.explanation: Builds resolve dependencies at that moment, even when source matches.

items.prompt: What risk do environment-parity practices close?
choices: Slow network links between several data centers
Missing comments in code
Drift between what was tested and what runs
items.explanation: Parity means staging results apply to production.

items.prompt: Staging and production jobs each run the build command on one commit. A dependency publishes a patch between the runs. What is now true?
choices: Both run identical code, since the commit matches
Production may run code that staging never tested
Staging runs newer code than production, safely
Neither build can succeed with a new patch
items.explanation: The second build resolves the newer version, so the tested and shipped artifacts differ.
items.reference:
Same box, every room
📦 build the artifact once
🏪 staging runs that artifact
🚚 production runs the same artifact
🔁 a rebuild per environment can drift
Why: same commit means same source, not the same build output.
items.learnMore:
Source versus build output

Two builds of one commit can resolve a dependency differently, run on different tool versions, or read different settings. Promoting one artifact makes the staging result a claim about the thing that ships.

Common mistake

Assuming a matching commit hash means a matching artifact.
items.reflection: Think of a sealed sample sent for inspection versus one repacked later. How do you know the inspected one is the one delivered?

items.prompt: Which design supports 'it passed staging, so this exact thing is in production'?
choices: Rebuild in production from the passing commit
Build in staging, then copy the source to production
Run the staging tests twice on one machine
Build once, then promote the same artifact ID
items.explanation: Only a single artifact moved through both gives that guarantee.
items.reference:
Same box, every room
📦 build the artifact once
🏪 staging runs that artifact
🚚 production runs the same artifact
🔁 a rebuild per environment can drift
Why: same commit means same source, not the same build output.

items.prompt: Why promote by artifact identity rather than by commit hash?
choices: Commits name the source; artifacts name the build
Commit hashes are changed again on every deploy
Artifacts are always smaller than the commits
Hashes cannot be shown on most pipeline dashboards
items.explanation: A hash pins the input. The artifact pins the output that was tested.

items.prompt: A build embeds an environment variable at build time, so builds differ per environment. Which fix removes the risk?
choices: Build twice and compare the two sets of settings by hand
Pin the runner and rebuild per environment
Build once and supply environment settings at run time
Build in production first and copy to staging
items.explanation: Moving environment-specific settings out of the build lets one artifact serve every environment.

Source versus build output

Two builds of one commit can resolve a dependency differently, run on different tool versions, or read different settings. Promoting one artifact makes the staging result a claim about the thing that ships.

Common mistake

Assuming a matching commit hash means a matching artifact.
items.reflection: Think of a sealed sample sent for inspection versus one repacked later. How do you know the inspected one is the one delivered?

items.prompt: When should the rollback path be decided?
choices: During the incident
After the postmortem
Before an incident
items.explanation: Under pressure is the worst time to invent it.

items.prompt: What should stay readily deployable to enable rollback?
choices: The next feature branch
The previous artifact
The staging database
items.explanation: Rolling back means redeploying the last good build.

items.prompt: A rehearsed rollback usually takes about how long?
choices: Minutes
Days
Fortnights
items.explanation: A rehearsed path is fast because nothing has to be figured out.

items.prompt: While broken code stays live, what keeps growing?
choices: The size of the source code base
The number of users who hit it
The test coverage
items.explanation: Every request meanwhile reaches the bad version.

items.prompt: At 50 users per minute, how many hit the bad deploy during a 5 minute rollback?
items.explanation: 5 minutes x 50 users per minute is 250.

items.prompt: Which is riskier?
choices: Improvising rollback mid-incident
Rehearsing the rollback beforehand
Keeping the old artifact
items.explanation: Improvising adds unknowns under pressure.

items.prompt: Why is an unrehearsed rollback slow?
choices: Rollbacks always need a brand new build
Nobody knows if the script still works
Staging blocks every rollback
items.explanation: An untested path hides surprises.

items.prompt: What makes recovery less of a guessing exercise?
choices: Repeatable deployment steps
More meetings during the incident
Fewer tests before release
items.explanation: Repeatable steps mean the path is already known.

items.prompt: A rollback takes 30 minutes while 50 users per minute hit the bad deploy. How many users are affected before it finishes?
items.explanation: 30 x 50 = 1,500. The cost is minutes times users per minute.
items.reference:
Cost grows with rollback time
⏱️ users affected = minutes x users per minute
🔁 keep the previous artifact deployable
🧪 rehearse the path before it is needed
📈 50 per minute: 5 min is 250, 30 min is 1,500
Why: a rehearsed rollback shrinks the one factor you control.
items.learnMore:
Decide before it burns

Every minute the broken version is live adds users in proportion. An improvised rollback also adds unknowns, like whether the old version and its script still work.

Common mistake

Treating rollback as something to figure out when it is needed.
items.reflection: Think of a fire exit plan. What changes between rehearsing it calmly and inventing it when the alarm sounds?

items.prompt: Pipeline configuration is what?
choices: Code that lives in the repository
A comment that the tools ignore completely
A log written by the server
items.explanation: Config is versioned and reviewable like code.

items.prompt: A deploy-gate change has what kind of blast radius?
choices: Always zero, since it ships nothing
Exactly the same as a styling change
Often a larger one than feature code
items.explanation: It decides what every later commit may ship.

items.prompt: What should a review ask of an override?
choices: Is the commit message under 50 characters long?
Why is it here and when does it come out?
Who owns the office plants?
items.explanation: That question turns a leftover into a visible decision.

items.prompt: Where does a reviewer see a config change?
choices: Only in production logs
Only after an incident
In a visible diff
items.explanation: The diff shows the new line before it merges.

items.prompt: Would review likely have caught the leftover flag?
choices: Yes, as an open question
No, config cannot be reviewed
Only after production failed
items.explanation: A visible override invites the question.

items.prompt: Treating config as low-stakes is what?
choices: A best practice
A failure mode
A requirement
items.explanation: Low-stakes treatment lets risky lines through.

items.prompt: How long did the leftover flag sit in the config?
choices: Two hours
Two years
Two weeks
items.explanation: The unit's case: two weeks before the second failure.

items.prompt: Who should review pipeline config changes?
choices: Nobody at all, since config never ships
A teammate, like application code
Only the tool vendor
items.explanation: Same rigor as the code they gate.

items.prompt: A pull request changes one line in the deploy workflow, adding a bypass flag. Why deserves the closest look?
choices: It changes how the dashboard looks to everyone
It is one line, so the risk is one line only
It only affects the commits made by the author
It can change what every later commit may ship
items.explanation: A gate line has reach far beyond its size.
items.reference:
Config is code
📝 pipeline config lives in the repository
👀 a gate change shows up as a diff
💥 its blast radius covers every future commit
❓ ask: why is this here, when does it come out?
Why: a deploy-gate change often reaches further than most feature code.
items.learnMore:
Review what decides what ships

Config feels lower-stakes because it ships no feature. A bypass line decides what every later commit may ship, so it deserves the same questions as application code.

Common mistake

Skipping review because the change is only one line of configuration.
items.reflection: Think of settings nobody reads, like a thermostat schedule or a shared-calendar rule. Who reviews them, and what could a wrong one quietly cost?

items.prompt: A reviewer sees continue-on-error with no comment. Which review question helps most?
choices: Can this be written in fewer characters overall?
What does this tolerate, and when does it come out?
Why is this line indented with two spaces here?
Does this step also run on the author's laptop?
items.explanation: The best questions ask for the reason and the expiry, which the leftover lacked.

items.prompt: Implement `countFailures(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return how many steps have `passed` equal to false.
items.explanation: A failure is a step with `passed` false, whether or not it is bypassed. `filter` then `length` counts them.

items.prompt: Implement `failedNames(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return the names of the steps whose `passed` is false, in order.
items.explanation: Filter to failed steps, then map to their names. Order follows the input.

items.prompt: Implement `isAllGreen(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return true when no step has failed, bypassed or not.
items.explanation: `every` is true for an empty list and false as soon as one step failed. Bypass flags do not change whether a step failed.

items.prompt: Implement `firstFailure(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return the name of the first step with `passed` false, or null if none, ignoring bypass flags.
items.explanation: Scan in order and return at the first failed step. Return null when the loop finishes.

items.prompt: Implement `bypassedFailures(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return the names of steps that failed and have `bypass` true, in order.
items.explanation: These are the hidden failures: the ones the pipeline recorded but did not act on.

items.prompt: Implement `hasBypass(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return true when any step has `bypass` set to true.
items.explanation: `some` is false for an empty list and true as soon as one step carries the flag.

items.prompt: Implement `passedNames(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return the names of the steps that passed, in order.
items.explanation: Keep passed steps, then take their names.

items.prompt: Implement `blockingFailures(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. Return the names of steps that failed and have `bypass` false, in order.
items.explanation: A blocking failure is a failure nobody marked as bypassable. The first of these is where the pipeline halts.

items.prompt: Implement `stoppedAt(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. The pipeline halts at the first step that failed and has `bypass` false. Return that step's name, or null if the pipeline never halts.

tests.description: incident: bypassed test does not stop

items.explanation: Failures are ignored only when bypassed, so the first failed step without a bypass is the stop point. A bypassed failure never returns.
items.reference:
The gate rule in one line
✅ a passed step: continue
🛑 a failed, non-bypassable step: halt here
🏳️ a failed, bypassable step: record, continue
🔎 the stop point is the first blocking failure
Why: the pipeline halts at the first step that fails and cannot be bypassed.
items.learnMore:
A small rule with big effects

Writing the rule as code forces the edge cases into the open: a failure that is recorded but ignored, an empty pipeline, a bypass on the first step.

Common mistake

Treating any failure as a stop, which forgets what a bypass changes.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist where some items are advisory. How would you write the rule for when the whole checklist stops?

items.prompt: Implement `stepsRun(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. The pipeline runs steps in order and halts after the first step that failed with `bypass` false (that step still ran). Return the names of the steps that ran.
items.explanation: Record the step before deciding to halt, because the blocking step itself ran. Break only on a failure that is not bypassed.

items.prompt: Implement `hiddenFailures(steps)`. Each step is `{ name, passed, bypass }`. The pipeline halts after the first blocking failure (failed, `bypass` false). Return the names of bypassed steps that failed and actually ran, in order.
items.explanation: Walk in order and stop at the first blocking failure, so steps after it never count. Bypassed failures before that point are the ones the dashboard hid.
